[[File:GCHQ-doughnut.jpg|thumb|Original scale model of the Doughnut, the proposed new headquarters building for [[GCHQ]].]]
'''The Doughnut''' is the nickname given (due to its resemblance to a [[doughnut]]) to the headquarters of the [[Government Communications Headquarters]] (GCHQ),<ref name=GCHQ>{{Cite web|title=Locations - Cheltenham|url=https://www.GCHQ.gov.uk/section/locations/cheltenham|website=www.GCHQ.gov.uk|location=[[Cheltenham]], Gloucestershire|publisher=[[GCHQ]]|date=2021|access-date=11 October 2021}}</ref><ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/> a British [[cryptography]] and [[intelligence agency]].  It is located on a {{Convert|176|acre|ha|disp=flip|abbr=off|lk=on}} site in [[Benhall, Cheltenham|Benhall]], in the suburbs of [[Cheltenham]], Gloucestershire, in [[South West England]].<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10>{{Cite web|last=Norton-Taylor|first=Richard|date=10 June 2003|url=https://www.TheGuardian.com/uk/2003/jun/10/terrorism.Whitehall|title=The Doughnut, the less secretive weapon in the fight against international terrorism|website=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=15 December 2013}}</ref><ref name=BBCAug11>{{Cite news|last=Whitworth|first=Tom|date=11 August 2011|url=https://www.BBC.co.uk/news/newsbeat-14589956|title=Inside the UK's top secret GCHQ base in Cheltenham|website=www.BBC.co.uk|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>  The Doughnut accommodates 5,500 employees; GCHQ is the largest single employer in Gloucestershire.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/><ref name=BBCAug11/><ref name=TelegOct14>{{Cite news|last=Moore|first=Charles|date=11 October 2014|url=https://www.Telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/defence/11154322/GCHQ-This-is-not-Blitz-Britain.-We-sure-as-hell-cant-lick-terrorism-on-our-own.html|title=GCHQ: 'This is not Blitz Britain. We sure as hell can't lick terrorism on our own'|website=www.Telegraph.co.uk|publisher=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|access-date=11 October 2014}}</ref>  Built to modernise and consolidate GCHQ's multiple buildings in Cheltenham, the Doughnut was completed in 2003, with GCHQ staff moving in the same year,<ref name=GCHQ/> and fully moved into the building in 2004.<ref name=GCHQWork>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gchq.gov.uk/how_we_work/running_the_business/Pages/Working-environment.aspx|title=Working environment|website=www.GCHQ.gov.uk|publisher=[[GCHQ]]|access-date=17 December 2013|archive-date=19 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219030836/http://www.gchq.gov.uk/how_we_work/running_the_business/Pages/Working-environment.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The Doughnut was too small for the number of staff at its completion, and a second building in a secret and undisclosed location in the 'Gloucestershire area' now also accommodates staff from GCHQ.  The Doughnut is surrounded by car and bicycle parking in concentric rings,<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/> and is well protected by security fencing, guards, and CCTV systems.

The construction of the building was financed by a [[private finance initiative]], and construction costs were greatly increased after difficulties in transferring computer infrastructure to the building.  The building is modern in design, and built primarily from steel, aluminium, and stone.<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/>  GCHQ management aspired for the building to be as well known internationally as [[the Pentagon]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.Telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1374817/Plans-for-new-GCHQ-go-on-view-to-public.html|title=Plans for new GCHQ go on view to public|website=www.Telegraph.co.uk|date=19 November 2000 |publisher=[[The Daily Telegraph]]}}</ref>

==Background==
The construction of the Doughnut in 2003 consolidated the operations previously spread across two sites into a single location, replacing more than 50 buildings in the process.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  The last staff from the nearby GCHQ site at [[Oakley, Gloucestershire|Oakley]] were transferred to the Doughnut in late 2011.<ref name=BBCDec11>{{Cite web|last=Knibbs|first=Steve|date=21 December 2011|url=https://www.BBC.co.uk/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-16290383|title=A final look at GCHQ's top secret Oakley site in Cheltenham|website=www.BBC.co.uk|location=[[Cheltenham]], Gloucestershire|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=11 October 2021}}</ref>

The design of the Doughnut reflects GCHQ's intended new mode of work after the end of the [[Cold War]], with its design facilitating talking among staff, and between them and the Director of GCHQ and his subordinates.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  It was estimated that anyone in the building could reach any other worker within five minutes.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  The director of GCHQ has no office; in 2014 director [[Iain Lobban]] described his desk as being located "within the shouting distance of lawyers".<ref name=TelegOct14/>

At a cost of £330&nbsp;million, the construction of the Doughnut was funded by a [[private finance initiative]] (PFI) put forward by a collective that included the British facilities management and construction company [[Carillion]] (now defunct), the Danish security company Group 4 / Falck (now [[G4S]]), and the British telecommunications company [[BT Group]].<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  The creation of the Doughnut was the largest PFI project to date for the British government.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  The building was designed by the British architect Chris Johnson for the American architectural firm [[Gensler]],<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/> and built by [[Carillion]].<ref name="Caril">{{Cite web|url=http://www.carillionplc.com/media/3827/_gchq_.pdf|title=GCHQ|website=www.Carillionplc.com|publisher=[[Carillion|Carillion plc]]|access-date=4 August 2014|archive-date=27 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160427063938/http://www.carillionplc.com/media/3827/_gchq_.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2004, [[Edward Leigh]], the chairman of the [[Commons Public Accounts Committee]], criticised the increasing cost of GCHQ's move to the Doughnut.<ref name=BBCJun04>{{Cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/gloucestershire/3807237.stm|title=MPs condemn spiraling GCHQ costs|website=News.BBC.co.uk|date=15 June 2004|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>  Leigh said that "It was astonishing GCHQ did not realise the extent of what would be involved much sooner".<ref name=BBCJun04/>  Leigh had said in 2003 that GCHQ's original estimate for the cost of the move was "staggeringly inaccurate".<ref name=BBCJul03>{{Cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/gloucestershire/3069501.stm|title=GCHQ criticised for huge move overspend|website=News.BBC.co.uk|date=16 July 2003|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>

For security reasons, GCHQ moved its own computers and technical infrastructure to the Doughnut, which caused the cost of its move to increase from £41&nbsp;million to £450&nbsp;million over two years.<ref name=BBCJun04/>  The moves of [[MI5]] and the [[Secret Intelligence Service]] (SIS) to new buildings had also cost more than three times their original estimates due to issues with transferring computers.<ref name="Aldrich, 2011, 497">{{harvnb|Aldrich|2011|p=497}}</ref>  [[HM Treasury]] paid £216&nbsp;million toward a newly agreed budget of £308&nbsp;million, having initially refused to finance the original high figure.<ref name=BBCJun04/>  The final cost of GCHQ's move to their new headquarters was more than seven times the original estimate.<ref name=BBCJul03/>

The complexity of the computer network at GCHQ was responsible for the increase in costs.  Issues with the network were found while preparing computers for the '[[Year 2000 problem|Millennium bug]]'.  Simply shutting down each computer individually before restarting them in the Doughnut would have left GCHQ unable to complete key intelligence work for two years, while moving their electronics according to the original schedule without "unacceptable damage" to intelligence gathering would cost £450&nbsp;million.<ref name=BBCJul03/>  In a review of GCHQ's move in 2003, the [[National Audit Office (United Kingdom)|National Audit Office]] (NAO) said government ministers might never have approved the consolidation of facilities had the final cost been known.<ref name=BBCJul03/>

==Design==
[[File:GCHQ from Leckhampton Hill.jpg|thumb|220px|The Doughnut from [[Leckhampton Hill and Charlton Kings Common|Leckhampton Hill]], 2010]]
The Doughnut is divided into three separate four-storey structures, identical in design, and connected at the top and bottom.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/><ref name=Gensler>{{Cite web|url=http://www.Gensler.com/project/government-communication-headquarters-gchq|title=Government Communication Headquarters (GCHQ)|website=www.Gensler.com|publisher=[[Gensler]]|access-date=17 December 2013}}{{Dead link|date=March 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>  With a total floor area of {{Convert|1500000|sqft|m2|disp=flip|abbr=off|lk=on}}, the building contains two circular blocks, internally divided by a 'street' covered in glass.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/><ref name=Gensler/>  Construction materials were primarily steel, aluminium, and stone,<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/> particularly granite and local [[limestone]] from the [[Cotswolds]]; designers incorporated recycled materials in the steelwork and the construction of desks.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  The design of the Doughnut was subsequently nominated for an award to "highlight improvements to the built and landscaped environment" given by Cheltenham's Civic Society.<ref name=GEOct11>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Beautiful-buildings-nominated-awards/story-13542304-detail/story.html|title=Beautiful buildings to be nominated for awards|website=www.GloucestershireEcho.co.uk|date=13 October 2011|publisher=[[Gloucestershire Echo]]|access-date=11 July 2014|archive-date=14 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714164458/http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Beautiful-buildings-nominated-awards/story-13542304-detail/story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

A circular walkway named The Street runs throughout the building.<ref name=BBCMar10>{{Cite web|last=Savage|first=Mark|date=29 March 2010|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/magazine/8589664.stm|title=Inside GCHQ: 'Caution: Here comes the BBC'|website=News.BBC.co.uk|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=28 December 2013}}</ref>  An open-air garden courtyard lies in the middle of the Doughnut; this garden is large enough to contain the [[Royal Albert Hall]].<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/>  The courtyard has a memorial to GCHQ staff who have been killed on active service; some five staff died in the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|War in Afghanistan]].<ref name=TelegOct14/>  Below the garden are banks of [[supercomputer]]s.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  The Doughnut is {{Convert|70|ft|m|abbr=off|lk=on|disp=flip}} high and {{Convert|600|ft|m|disp=flip|abbr=off}} in diameter.<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/>  Individual spaces in the Doughnut include the GCHQ archive holding 16&nbsp;million historical artefacts,<ref name=GCHQ/> and the 24/7 operations centre<ref name=GCHQ/> where people working in "small 12-hour shifts monitor GCHQ systems and news bulletins."<ref name=TelegOct14/>  The 'Action On' programme enables the 24/7 staff to act "quickly and freely" to supply information to [[British Armed Forces]] to help their operations.<ref name=TelegOct14/>  The Doughnut's internet operations centre (INOC), is where "the best technical capabilities [are matched] with the most urgent operational requirements" according to [[Charles Moore (journalist)|Charles Moore]] who visited the Doughnut in 2014 for ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]''.<ref name=TelegOct14/>

The structure of the Doughnut is designed to minimise any potential effect of a fire or a terrorist attack on the building; it also includes independent power generators which can supply power to the facilities in an emergency.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  About {{Convert|1850|mi|km|abbr=off|lk=on|sigfig=1}} of [[fibre optics]] were installed in the Doughnut by [[British Telecom]], and about {{Convert|6000|mi|km|sigfig=1|abbr=off}} of electrical wiring were used in the building.<ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>

The Doughnut is surrounded by car and bicycle parking in concentric rings, guarded by a two-metre metal fence and half a dozen vehicle checkpoints.<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/><ref name=BBCAug11/>  The Doughnut is served by an underground road.<ref name=BBC-2003-06-22/>

Facilities available to staff at the Doughnut include a 600-seat restaurant, cafes, shops, a gymnasium, and a prayer or quiet room.<ref name=GCHQ/><ref name=Guardian2003-06-10/>  Exhibits from the history of GCHQ are displayed throughout the building, including the radios used by the [[Portland spy ring]].<ref name=BBCMar10/>

==History==
[[File:GCHQ at Cheltenham, Gloucestershire MOD 45154333.jpg|thumb|Movable satellite receiver dish in front of the [[GCHQ]] Doughnut]]
The Doughnut was officially opened in 2004 by [[Queen Elizabeth II]], accompanied by the [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh|Duke of Edinburgh]].<ref name=GENov3013>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/GCHQ-gets-Royal-visit-London-office/story-20244490-detail/story.html|title=GCHQ gets Royal visit at London office|website=www.GloucestershireEcho.co.uk|date=30 November 2013|publisher=[[Gloucestershire Echo]]|access-date=11 July 2014|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924023006/http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/GCHQ-gets-Royal-visit-London-office/story-20244490-detail/story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>  In 2008, the then [[Labour Party (United Kingdom)|Labour]] [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom]], [[Gordon Brown]], visited the Doughnut and praised the staff working there in a speech.<ref name=GEOct08>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Prime-Minister-visited-GCHQ-Cheltenham/story-11892990-detail/story.html|title=Prime Minister visited GCHQ in Cheltenham|website=www.GloucestershireEcho.co.uk|date=11 October 2008|publisher=[[Gloucestershire Echo]]|access-date=11 July 2014|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924023100/http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Prime-Minister-visited-GCHQ-Cheltenham/story-11892990-detail/story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Doughnut has been visited three times by the then [[Charles, Prince of Wales]] since its opening.<ref name=BBCMar11>{{Cite web|url=https://www.BBC.co.uk/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-12623275|title=Prince Charles and Camilla visit GCHQ in Cheltenham|website=www.BBC.co.uk|date=3 March 2011|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>  Charles was accompanied by [[Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall]] in 2011, on his second visit to the Doughnut.<ref name=BBCMar11/>

The Doughnut was already too small for the number of GCHQ staff at its completion, as a vast expansion in the number of employees had occurred as a consequence of the [[September 11 attacks]] in 2001.<ref name="Aldrich, 2011, 9" >{{harvnb|Aldrich|2011|p=9}}</ref>  The staff numbered almost 6,500 by 2008.<ref name="Aldrich, 2011, 9"/>  The addition of a two-storey office block and a three-storey car park to the Doughnut was proposed in 2008, but eventually suspended in 2011.<ref name=GEAug1411>{{Cite web|url=http://www.GloucesterCitizen.co.uk/GCHQ-plans-shelved-new-site-staff-identified/story-13131141-detail/story.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140711190507/http://www.gloucestercitizen.co.uk/GCHQ-plans-shelved-new-site-staff-identified/story-13131141-detail/story.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=11 July 2014|title=GCHQ plans shelved as new site for staff identified|website=www.GloucesterCitizen.co.uk|date=14 August 2011|publisher=[[Gloucestershire Echo]]|access-date=11 July 2014}}</ref>  The new buildings were intended to facilitate the arrival of 800 staff from GCHQ's former site at [[Oakley, Gloucestershire|Oakley]].<ref name=GEAug1411/>  Though it was initially felt that the Doughnut would be adequate for the new staff, 600 contractors working on technical projects for GCHQ were eventually relocated to a secret undisclosed building in the 'Gloucestershire area'.<ref name=GEAug1411/>  The parking of cars by GCHQ staff on residential roads has caused 'annoyance' among local residents in Benhall.<ref name=GEAug1411/>  It was believed that the arrival of new staff may have further affected local parking, but GCHQ stated the presence of the new employees would have been offset by redundancies.<ref name=GEAug1411/>

On 1 June 2007, the building and its grounds were designated as a protected site for the purposes of Section 128 of the [[Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005]].  The effect of the act was to make it a specific criminal offence for a person to [[Trespass in English law|trespass]] into the site.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.GOV.uk/government/publications/trespass-on-protected-sites-sections-128-131-of-the-serious-organised-crime-and-police-act-2005|title=Home Office Circular 018 / 2007 (Trespass on protected sites – sections 128–131 of the Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005)|website=www.GOV.uk|date=22 May 2007|publisher=[[Government of the United Kingdom]]|access-date=18 July 2017}}</ref>

Access to the Doughnut is rarely granted to representatives from the media, but it was visited for the March 2010 [[BBC Radio 4]] documentary ''GCHQ: Cracking the Code'',<ref name=BBCMar10/> by [[Charles Moore (journalist)|Charles Moore]] for an interview with GCHQ director [[Iain Lobban]] for ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' in October 2014,<ref name=TelegOct14/> and by historian and writer [[Ben Macintyre]] who visited the Doughnut for a series of articles for ''[[The Times]]'' in October 2015 in anticipation of the draft [[Investigatory Powers Act 2016|Investigatory Powers Bill]].<ref name=TimesOct15>{{Cite news|last=Macintyre|first=Ben|date=28 October 2015|title=For your eyes only|url=|work=[[The Times]]|issue=71740|page=1}}</ref>

===Charitable efforts===
[[File:GCHQ lit in rainbow on 2015 IDAHOT.jpg|thumb|GCHQ illuminated in [[Rainbow flag (LGBT movement)|rainbow spectrum of colours]] to mark the [[International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia]] in 2015]]
Originally an annual event, a Community Day is held at the Doughnut to highlight the charitable and volunteer work by GCHQ staff in the local Cheltenham community.<ref name=GCHQNov13>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gchq.gov.uk/press_and_media/news_and_features/Pages/GCHQ-Community-Day-2013.aspx|title=GCHQ showcases its volunteering and charity work at Community Day 2013|website=www.GCHQ.gov.uk|location=[[Cheltenham]], Gloucestershire|date=8 November 2013|publisher=[[GCHQ]]|access-date=17 December 2013|archive-date=19 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219025105/http://www.gchq.gov.uk/press_and_media/news_and_features/Pages/GCHQ-Community-Day-2013.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref>  More recent Community Day events are held approximately every 18 months.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.GCHQ.gov.uk/section/culture/giving-back|title=Culture - Giving back|website=www.GCHQ.gov.uk|location=[[Cheltenham]], Gloucestershire|publisher=[[GCHQ]]|date=2021|access-date=11 October 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.GCHQ.gov.uk/information/community-day-2017|title=Community Day 2017|website=www.GCHQ.gov.uk|location=[[Cheltenham]], Gloucestershire|publisher=[[GCHQ]]|date=8 December 2017|access-date=11 October 2021}}</ref>

In October 2014, 1,308 GCHQ staff formed a giant [[Papaver rhoeas|red poppy]] in the Doughnut's central courtyard to mark the start of the [[Royal British Legion]]'s (RBL) [[Remembrance poppy#United Kingdom|Poppy Appeal]].<ref name=BBCOct14>{{Cite news|url=https://www.BBC.co.uk/news/uk-england-gloucestershire-29745303|title=Giant poppy made by 1,400 GCHQ intelligence agency staff|website=www.BBC.co.uk|date=24 October 2014|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=24 October 2014}}</ref>  The poppy was {{Convert|38|m|abbr=off}} in size with a {{Convert|28|m|abbr=off}} long stalk.<ref name=BBCOct14/>  The staff wore red [[Poncho|rain ponchos]], with the black centre of the poppy formed by the uniforms of [[Royal Navy]] personnel.<ref name=BBCOct14/>

In 2015, the Doughnut was illuminated with yellow light to mark GCHQ staff's support for [[The Guide Dogs for the Blind Association]],<ref name=GEOct715>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/GCHQ-turns-doughnut-yellow-support-Guide-Dogs/story-27940985-detail/story.html|title=GCHQ turns the Cheltenham 'doughnut' yellow to show support for Guide Dogs|website=www.GloucestershireEcho.co.uk|date=7 October 2015|publisher=[[Gloucestershire Echo]]|access-date=10 February 2016|archive-date=11 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151011220622/http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/GCHQ-turns-doughnut-yellow-support-Guide-Dogs/story-27940985-detail/story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> and by a [[Rainbow flag (LGBT movement)|rainbow spectrum of colours]] to mark the [[International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia]].<ref name=GEMay1715>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Iconic-GCHQ-donut-lit-like-rainbow-tonight/story-26514632-detail/story.html|title=GCHQ to be lit up like a rainbow for International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia|website=www.GloucestershireEcho.co.uk|date=17 May 2015|publisher=[[Gloucestershire Echo]]|access-date=10 February 2016|archive-date=22 December 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222053837/http://www.gloucestershireecho.co.uk/Iconic-GCHQ-donut-lit-like-rainbow-tonight/story-26514632-detail/story.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In early 2018, the Doughnut among others was again lit up in rainbow colours in support of LGBTQ causes.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/article/gchq-signals-pride-in-its-gay-spooks-sg6lpxz970f|title=GCHQ signals pride in its gay spooks|website=[[The Times]]}}</ref>

The three other headquarters of British intelligence agencies;
*The [[SIS Building]] – headquarters of the [[Secret Intelligence Service]] (SIS), known as MI6
*[[Thames House]] – headquarters of the [[MI5|Security Service]], known as MI5
*[[Northwood Headquarters]] and [[Ministry of Defence Main Building (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence Main Building]] – headquarters of the [[British Armed Forces]] and the [[Defence Intelligence]] (DI)
